Title: The efficacy and safety of electro-acupuncture for alleviating chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy in patients with coloreactal cancer: study protocol for a single-blinded, randomized sham-controlled trial.
Abstract: BACKGROUND: Colorectal cancer is the most common cancer in Hong Kong. Oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy is a major first-line conventional therapy for advanced and metastatic colorectal cancer. However, oxaliplatin causes chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN). Acupuncture has long been used to alleviate limb numbness in Chinese medicine. This study aims to examine the efficacy and safety of acupuncture for alleviating CIPN in patients with colorectal cancer in Hong Kong. METHODS/DESIGN: This is a single-blinded, randomized, sham-controlled efficacy trial. Eighty-four eligible patients, who are Hong Kong Chinese, aged ≥ 18 years, diagnosed with colorectal cancer and undergoing oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy, will be randomized in a ratio of 1:1 to the electro-acupuncture group or the sham-controlled group. During a 12-week treatment period, patients in the electro-acupuncture group will undergo electro-acupuncture once a week from the first cycle of chemotherapy, while patients in the control group will receive sham acupuncture, and the patients in both groups will be followed up for 12 weeks. The primary outcome measure is the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy/Gynecologic Oncology Group-Neurotoxicity (FACT/GOC-Ntx) questionnaire. The secondary outcome measures include numerical rating scale (NRS) for numbness/pain, vibration and light touch sense test, the European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire-C30 (EORTC QLQ-C30) and Constitution of Chinese Medicine Questionnaire (CCMQ). DISCUSSION: The study will compare electro-acupuncture with sham acupuncture to explore the feasibility for electro-acupuncture in improving symptoms caused by chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinicaltrials.gov, NCT03582423. Registered on 11 July 2018.
Abstract_Summary: This study looks at people in Hong Kong. They have colon or rectum cancer. They get a drug named oxaliplatin. This drug can make hands and feet feel odd. They may feel numb, weak, or have pins and needles. The study asks: can needles help this? The “needle care” is called acupuncture. It has been used in China for many years. Eighty‑four grown ups will join the study. All are Chinese and live in Hong Kong. All get oxaliplatin for their cancer care. They go into two groups by chance. One group gets real electro‑acupuncture each week. A small tool sends soft buzz to the needles. The other group gets “pretend” acupuncture. The pretend care looks real but should not work. Both groups get care for 12 weeks. Then they are watched for 12 more weeks. The team will use forms with many questions. These forms ask about numb feel and pain. They also test touch and feel in the skin. They ask about daily life and mood. The goal is to see if real acupuncture helps. They also check that it is safe to use. If it helps, it may be used more. It may give people more ease in hands and feet.
Full_Text_Summary_With_In_Text_Citations: This study looks at people in Hong Kong who have bowel cancer and get a drug called oxaliplatin as part of their chemo treatment (Abstract, para. 1). Many of these people get nerve pain and numb hands and feet from this drug, which can make daily life hard (Introduction, para. 1). We want to see if a treatment called acupuncture can safely help ease this numbness and pain (Abstract, para. 1). This may help adults with stage II to IV bowel cancer who are starting oxaliplatin and do not already have nerve problems (Methods, para. 2). In the study, 84 adults will join and we will split them into two groups by chance, like a coin toss (Abstract, para. 2). One group will get real electric acupuncture once a week for 12 weeks, and the other group will get a “sham” treatment where the needles do not go into the skin (Abstract, para. 2). We will ask people questions about their nerve symptoms and pain each week and for 12 more weeks after treatment ends (Methods, para. 1). We will then compare the two groups to see if real acupuncture works better than sham treatment for chemo nerve problems (Abstract, para. 3). If it helps, this could lead to larger studies and may offer a non-drug way to ease nerve pain from chemo in the future (Discussion, para. 1).
